facts.text: A lawyer: dry, loyal, slow to judge, and often the last friend of men going downhill.
facts.quote: it was frequently his fortune to be the last reputable acquaintance and the last good influence in the lives of downgoing men

facts.text: Already knows whose name was on the cheque, and asks Enfield to be exact.
facts.quote: if I do not ask you the name of the other party, it is because I know it already

facts.text: Keeps Dr. Jekyll’s will in his safe and has always hated it.
facts.quote: This document had long been the lawyer’s eyesore.

facts.text: Decides to find Hyde by watching the door.
facts.quote: I shall be Mr. Seek.

facts.text: Identifies the murdered man as his client Sir Danvers Carew.
facts.quote: I am sorry to say that this is Sir Danvers Carew.

facts.text: Locks away Hyde’s letter after Guest finds the hand like Jekyll’s, and suspects forgery.
facts.quote: Henry Jekyll forge for a murderer!

facts.text: Holds Lanyon’s sealed packet, to be opened only on Jekyll’s death or disappearance.
facts.quote: not to be opened till the death or disappearance of Dr. Henry Jekyll.

facts.text: Breaks into the cabinet with Poole and finds a new will naming himself.
facts.quote: read the name of Gabriel John Utterson

facts.text: Objected to the will from the start, as Jekyll acknowledges.
facts.quote: I next drew up that will to which you so much objected

facts.text: Utterson’s distant kinsman and Sunday walking companion.
facts.quote: Mr. Richard Enfield, his distant kinsman, the well-known man about town.

facts.text: Saw a small man trample a child at three in the morning and made him pay.
facts.quote: the man trampled calmly over the child’s body and left her screaming on the ground.

facts.text: Names the man.
facts.quote: It was a man of the name of Hyde.

facts.text: Has worked out that the door is a back way into Dr. Jekyll’s house.
facts.quote: this was a back way to Dr. Jekyll’s

facts.text: Jekyll recognises him as the passerby who stopped Hyde after the child.
facts.quote: whom I recognised the other day in the person of your kinsman

library.note: Your highlight: “I had worked hard for nearly two years, for the sole purpose of infusing life into an inanimate body.”

facts.text: A small man who trampled a child and paid with a cheque signed by someone well known.
facts.quote: a cheque for the balance on Coutts’s, drawn payable to bearer and signed with a name that I can’t mention

facts.text: Gives everyone a feeling of deformity that no one can pin down.
facts.quote: He must be deformed somewhere; he gives a strong feeling of deformity, although I couldn’t specify the point.

facts.text: Named in Dr. Jekyll’s will as heir to everything, even if Jekyll merely disappears.
facts.quote: the said Edward Hyde should step into the said Henry Jekyll’s shoes without further delay

facts.text: Has a key to the door; gives Utterson an address in Soho.
facts.quote: And he gave a number of a street in Soho.

facts.text: Pale, dwarfish, with a husky whispering voice.
facts.quote: Mr. Hyde was pale and dwarfish, he gave an impression of deformity without any nameable malformation

facts.text: Jekyll’s servants have orders to obey him.
facts.quote: We have all orders to obey him.

facts.text: Jekyll says he can be rid of him whenever he chooses.
facts.quote: the moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr. Hyde.

facts.text: Beats Sir Danvers Carew to death with a cane, seen by a maid.
facts.quote: Mr. Hyde broke out of all bounds and clubbed him to the earth.

facts.text: His Soho rooms are found ransacked, papers burned, the other half of the stick behind the door.
facts.quote: the other half of the stick was found behind the door

facts.text: His handwriting is nearly Jekyll’s, only sloped the other way.
facts.quote: the two hands are in many points identical: only differently sloped.

facts.text: Vanishes after the murder.
facts.quote: Mr. Hyde had disappeared out of the ken of the police as though he had never existed.

facts.text: Found dead in Jekyll’s cabinet, in Jekyll’s clothes, a crushed phial in his hand.
facts.quote: turned it on its back and beheld the face of Edward Hyde.

facts.text: Lanyon saw him drink a draught and turn into Henry Jekyll.
facts.quote: The creature who crept into my house that night was, on Jekyll’s own confession, known by the name of Hyde

facts.text: Jekyll’s own evil nature, given a body by a drug.
facts.quote: Edward Hyde, alone in the ranks of mankind, was pure evil.

facts.text: A doctor of many titles whose will leaves everything to Edward Hyde.
facts.quote: in case of the decease of Henry Jekyll, M.D., D.C.L., LL.D., F.R.S., etc., all his possessions were to pass into the hands of his

facts.text: Lanyon says he went wrong in mind more than ten years ago.
facts.quote: it is more than ten years since Henry Jekyll became too fanciful for me.

facts.text: His house is in a square; Hyde comes and goes by the laboratory behind it.
facts.quote: he mostly comes and goes by the laboratory.

facts.text: Fifty, large and smooth-faced, fond of Utterson.
facts.quote: a large, well-made, smooth-faced man of fifty

facts.text: Asks Utterson to promise to protect Hyde’s rights if he is gone.
facts.quote: I only ask you to help him for my sake, when I am no longer here.

facts.text: Swears he is done with Hyde for ever.
facts.quote: I swear to God I will never set eyes on him again.

facts.text: After two months of good health, shuts himself away and asks Utterson to respect his silence.
facts.quote: I mean from henceforth to lead a life of extreme seclusion

facts.text: Seen at his window, then struck by a look of terror.
facts.quote: an expression of such abject terror and despair

facts.text: Leaves Utterson a note: read Lanyon’s narrative, then his own confession.
facts.quote: first read the narrative which Lanyon warned me he was to place in your hands

facts.text: Appears in Lanyon’s consulting room where Hyde had stood.
facts.quote: there stood Henry Jekyll!

facts.text: His thesis: a man is two, not one.
facts.quote: man is not truly one, but truly two.

facts.text: Made a drug that gives the lower side of him a body of its own.
facts.quote: managed to compound a drug by which these powers should be dethroned from their supremacy

facts.text: The salt ran out; the fresh supply does not work; the first batch had an impurity.
facts.quote: it was that unknown impurity which lent efficacy to the draught.

facts.text: A great physician of Cavendish Square, old friend of Utterson and Jekyll.
facts.quote: the great Dr. Lanyon, had his house and received his crowding patients.

facts.text: Hearty, red-faced, hair white early.
facts.quote: a hearty, healthy, dapper, red-faced gentleman, with a shock of hair prematurely white

facts.text: Fell out with Jekyll over his science.
facts.quote: Such unscientific balderdash

facts.text: Has never heard of Hyde.
facts.quote: Never heard of him. Since my time.

facts.text: Jekyll calls him a hidebound pedant.
facts.quote: that hidebound pedant, Lanyon

facts.text: Has had a shock and says he will not recover.
facts.quote: I have had a shock

facts.text: Will not hear Jekyll’s name.
facts.quote: I am quite done with that person

facts.text: Dies within a fortnight, leaving a sealed packet for Utterson.
facts.quote: in something less than a fortnight he was dead.

facts.text: Fetched a drawer of powders from Jekyll’s cabinet, as a letter begged him to.
facts.quote: returned with it to Cavendish Square.

facts.text: Watched Hyde drink the draught and become Jekyll, and cannot bear what he saw.
facts.quote: I saw what I saw, I heard what I heard, and my soul sickened at it

facts.text: Jekyll’s elderly butler.
facts.quote: A well-dressed, elderly servant opened the door.

facts.text: Confirms that Hyde has a key.
facts.quote: Mr. Hyde has a key.

facts.text: Says no letter came by hand that day, only the post.
facts.quote: nothing had come except by post

facts.text: Reports the doctor shut in the cabinet, silent and low.
facts.quote: Poole had, indeed, no very pleasant news to communicate.

facts.text: Comes to Utterson at night, afraid of foul play.
facts.quote: I think there’s been foul play

facts.text: Twenty years in Jekyll’s service; sure the voice behind the door is not his master’s.
facts.quote: Have I been twenty years in this man’s house, to be deceived about his voice?

facts.text: Breaks the cabinet door with an axe.
facts.quote: Poole swung the axe over his shoulder

facts.text: Has orders to wait for Lanyon with a locksmith.
facts.quote: Poole, my butler, has his orders

facts.text: An aged, white-haired gentleman, beaten to death in a lane by Hyde.
facts.quote: an aged and beautiful gentleman with white hair

facts.text: Identified by Utterson.
facts.quote: this is Sir Danvers Carew.

facts.text: Was Utterson’s client.
facts.quote: Carew was my client

facts.text: A Member of Parliament, says the special edition.
facts.quote: Shocking murder of an M.P.

facts.text: A reward is offered; his death is felt as a public injury.
facts.quote: the death of Sir Danvers was resented as a public injury

facts.text: Jekyll says no sane man could have killed him on so small a provocation.
facts.quote: no man morally sane could have been guilty of that crime upon so pitiful a provocation

facts.text: Utterson’s head clerk, a student of handwriting.
facts.quote: a great student and critic of handwriting

facts.text: Finds Hyde’s hand and Jekyll’s nearly identical.
facts.quote: there’s a rather singular resemblance; the two hands are in many points identical

facts.text: Dines with Utterson while Jekyll’s door is shut.
facts.quote: The fifth night, he had in Guest to dine with him

facts.text: The Scotland Yard inspector on the Carew case.
facts.quote: This is Inspector Newcomen of Scotland Yard.

facts.text: Finds the burnt cheque book and the other half of the stick in Hyde’s rooms.
facts.quote: the butt end of a green cheque book

facts.text: Jekyll’s footman, sent to guard the laboratory door.
facts.quote: The footman came at the summons, very white and nervous.

facts.text: Once saw Hyde in the house at a strange hour, in clothes far too big.
facts.quote: Bradshaw stared and drew back at seeing Mr. Hyde at such an hour

facts.text: A blistered door without bell or knocker, in a sinister windowless block.
facts.quote: The door, which was equipped with neither bell nor knocker, was blistered and distained.

facts.text: Enfield calls it Black Mail House.
facts.quote: Black Mail House is what I call that place with the door

facts.text: Utterson watches it at all hours.
facts.quote: Mr. Utterson began to haunt the door in the bystreet of shops.

facts.text: It is the old dissecting room door of Jekyll’s house.
facts.quote: I saw Mr. Hyde go in by the old dissecting room door, Poole

facts.text: Enfield now knows it leads to Jekyll’s.
facts.quote: this was a back way to Dr. Jekyll’s

facts.text: Its key is found broken and rusted on the flags.
facts.quote: they found the key, already stained with rust.

facts.text: Jekyll locked it and crushed the key after the murder.
facts.quote: ground the key under my heel!

name: Soho
world: A district of London’s West End. In the 1880s it was crowded and poor, known for foreign eating houses, music halls and cheap lodgings.

facts.text: Hyde’s address.
facts.quote: And he gave a number of a street in Soho.

facts.text: Seen through fog, a district like a city in a nightmare.
facts.quote: The dismal quarter of Soho seen under these changing glimpses

facts.text: Hyde’s two rooms there are furnished with luxury.
facts.quote: Mr. Hyde had only used a couple of rooms; but these were furnished with luxury and good taste.

facts.text: Hyde was last seen leaving his Soho house on the morning of the murder.
facts.quote: From the time he had left the house in Soho on the morning of the murder, he was simply blotted out

facts.text: Jekyll took and furnished the Soho house himself.
facts.quote: I took and furnished that house in Soho, to which Hyde was tracked by the police

name: Cavendish Square
world: A garden square in Marylebone, London. By Stevenson’s day the streets around it, Harley Street among them, were lined with physicians’ houses.

facts.text: Lanyon’s house, in the citadel of medicine.
facts.quote: Cavendish Square, that citadel of medicine

facts.text: Where Jekyll’s letter asks Lanyon to bring the drawer.
facts.quote: carry back with you to Cavendish Square exactly as it stands.

facts.text: Lanyon brings the drawer home there.
facts.quote: returned with it to Cavendish Square.

facts.text: Written in Jekyll’s own hand; Utterson refused to help draft it.
facts.quote: The will was holograph, for Mr. Utterson, though he took charge of it now that it was made, had refused to lend the least assistance in the making of it

facts.text: Leaves everything to Hyde, even on a disappearance of three months.
facts.quote: the said Edward Hyde should step into the said Henry Jekyll’s shoes without further delay

facts.text: Jekyll knows Utterson is distressed by it and will not discuss it.
facts.quote: I never saw a man so distressed as you were by my will

facts.text: Hyde dictated the disappearance clause; Jekyll admits it with a nod.
facts.quote: it was Hyde who dictated the terms in your will about that disappearance?

facts.text: Utterson has long since returned it to Jekyll.
facts.quote: the mad will which he had long ago restored to its author

facts.text: A new will, in the same terms, names Utterson instead of Hyde.
facts.quote: in place of the name of Edward Hyde, the lawyer, with indescribable amazement, read the name of Gabriel John Utterson.

facts.text: Jekyll drew it up so he could carry on as Hyde without losing his money.
facts.quote: so that if anything befell me in the person of Dr. Jekyll, I could enter on that of Edward Hyde without pecuniary loss.

facts.text: Jekyll’s private room above the old dissecting theatre: glass presses, a cheval-glass, barred windows.
facts.quote: It was a large room, fitted round with glass presses, furnished, among other things, with a cheval-glass and a business table

facts.text: Jekyll now lives and sometimes sleeps there.
facts.quote: confined himself to the cabinet over the laboratory, where he would sometimes even sleep

facts.text: Jekyll has shut himself in again; Poole is afraid.
facts.quote: he’s shut up again in the cabinet

facts.text: Its red baize door gives way to Poole’s axe at the fifth blow.
facts.quote: it was not until the fifth, that the lock burst in sunder and the wreck of the door fell inwards on the carpet.

facts.text: Holds press E with the drawer of powders.
facts.quote: to open the glazed press (letter E) on the left hand

facts.text: Jekyll’s refuge when the change comes on him.
facts.quote: I had but the time to gain the shelter of my cabinet

library.note: Your note: “Both men hide the recipe from the reader on purpose.”

facts.text: Something Jekyll sends Poole to every chemist for, and rejects as impure.
facts.quote: This drug is wanted bitter bad, sir, whatever for.

facts.text: A note to Messrs. Maw begs for the old sample.
facts.quote: find me some of the old.

facts.text: A white salt in measured heaps on glass saucers in the cabinet.
facts.quote: various measured heaps of some white salt being laid on glass saucers

facts.text: In the drawer: powders, a phial and a paper book.
facts.quote: some powders, a phial and a paper book

facts.text: Mixed, it effervesces, turns dark purple, then watery green.
facts.quote: the compound changed to a dark purple, which faded again more slowly to a watery green

facts.text: Jekyll’s own compound, which lets a second form take over.
facts.quote: a second form and countenance substituted

facts.text: The first supply was impure, and only that impurity worked.
facts.quote: I am now persuaded that my first supply was impure

facts.text: Wholesale chemists Jekyll bought his salt from, years before.
facts.quote: Dr. Jekyll presents his compliments to Messrs. Maw.

facts.text: Their man threw the note back at Poole in anger.
facts.quote: The man at Maw’s was main angry, sir

name: Coutts’s
world: A private bank in the Strand, London, founded in 1692 and long the banker of the wealthy.

facts.text: The bank the cheque was drawn on.
facts.quote: a cheque for the balance on Coutts’s

name: Regent’s Park
world: A large royal park in north-west London, opened to the public in the 1830s.

facts.text: Where Jekyll, on a bench on a January day, turns into Hyde without the drug.
facts.quote: the Regent’s Park was full of winter chirrupings and sweet with spring odours.

facts.text: The surgeon whose theatre became Jekyll’s laboratory.
facts.quote: old Dr. Denman’s surgical theatre
